questions.q: What offer did Netflix make to Blockbuster in 2000?
a: To sell itself for $50 million and run its online service
To merge as equal partners in a new company
To buy Blockbuster's stores for $6 billion
To license its streaming technology
questions.why: Lesson 1 says Netflix offered to be bought for 50 million dollars, with Hastings running the online service.

questions.q: What three conditions does Hastings say must come first?
a: High talent density, candor and few pointless policies
Large teams, strict rules and long hours
Cheap salaries, loyalty and job security
Careful approvals, secrecy and clear hierarchy
questions.why: Lesson 2 lists talent density, lots of candor and throwing out pointless policies as the foundation.

questions.q: How does Netflix view its employees?
a: Like a sports team trying to win a title
Like a family that stays together always
Like students who need close supervision
Like contractors hired project by project
questions.why: Lesson 3 contrasts Netflix's sports-team view with companies that treat employees as family for life.

questions.q: What does radical candor look like at Netflix?
a: Employees openly disagree with supervisors
Feedback is shared only in annual reviews
Managers shield staff from criticism
Criticism is delivered anonymously
questions.why: Lesson 2 says contradicting a supervisor is normal and expected, and staying silent is seen as disloyal.

questions.q: Why does Netflix avoid tracking hours and vacations?
a: Freedom shows trust and creates accountability
It saves money on HR software
It makes legal compliance simpler
It prevents employees from taking leave
questions.why: Lesson 2 says dropping such policies shows employees they are trusted, which increases accountability.
